summary: This informational memo discusses the problem of securing real-time multimedia sessions. It explains why RTP and RTCP do not mandate a single media security mechanism, which matters to designers and reviewers of RTP extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries many kinds of real-time media, from private calls to large streams. RFC 7202 explains why each interoperable class of RTP application must choose security that fits its needs instead of requiring one mechanism for all RTP uses.

questions: why rtp has no mandatory security
why does rtp not mandate srtp
subtitle: Why RTP specifies different security choices for different kinds of media applications.

tldr.problem: RTP serves application scenarios with very different security and key-management needs. A single mandatory security mechanism would not fit every use of the framework.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends security building blocks and requires each interoperable class of RTP application to select mandatory-to-implement security appropriate to its scenario.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7202 is high-level guidance for designers of RTP specifications. It distinguishes application classes, payload formats, and profiles when deciding where security requirements belong.

today: RFC 7202 is an Informational IETF document. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it gives guidance on specifying security for RTP application classes and extensions.

sections.title: Different RTP Uses Have Different Needs
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries voice, television, video conferences, and other real-time or streaming media. These uses range from point-to-point sessions to large multicast groups and from low to high data rates. They may run over different transports and in networks with different trust and reliability properties.

RTP's base specification has limited media-security options and no standard key-exchange mechanism. RFC 7202 explains why multiple media-security and key-management mechanisms are appropriate for the framework rather than one mechanism for every application.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP is used by applications with very different communication patterns and security needs. A mechanism that fits one kind of call or stream may not fit another.

sections.title: Media Protection and Key Management
sections.content:
Secure RTP (SRTP) is described as a widely applicable option. It encrypts RTP media payloads but not RTP headers, and it can optionally support source-origin authentication. Its design aims for low overhead and support for RTP's group communication and monitoring features.

SRTP is not suitable for every scenario. The RFC gives ISMACryp payload-level confidentiality for some streaming-video applications as an example of an alternative that does not suit voice telephony. Key management also varies: some mechanisms operate in-band on the media path, while others operate out-of-band through session signaling. The RFC points to RFC 7201 for a survey of options available at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP protects media payloads while leaving RTP headers unencrypted, but it is not suitable for every application. Applications also need a way to establish sessions and exchange keys, and those needs vary too.

sections.title: Where Mandatory Security Belongs
sections.content:
The IETF's strong-security policy calls for mandatory-to-implement security so implementations can interoperate securely. RTP is a framework used by different application classes whose implementations are not necessarily expected to work together, and those classes have different security requirements.

A specification defining an interoperable class of RTP applications must select its mandatory security mechanisms. An RTP payload format describes how a codec's output is carried and can be used by many application classes, so it should discuss its security implications but should not mandate SRTP or another security building block for every use.

RTP profiles are broader extensions. A profile may mandate security when it defines a class with shared needs, but the RFC does not expect every profile to do so. A profile that does not define an interoperable application usage should explain that choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Specifications for a defined, interoperable application class must choose the security its implementations will support. A codec format used by many classes should not force one security choice on all of them.

sections.title: A Framework of Security Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that no single media-security or keying mechanism can be mandatory for all RTP uses. Each class of application needs an analysis of its security requirements and a selection of mandatory building blocks for media protection and key management.

The RFC expects a document for each interoperable application class to describe the security options that implementations must support. Its Security Considerations section states that the memo is about mandatory-to-implement security.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no single media-security solution for every RTP application. Each interoperable class needs a specification that names the security mechanisms its implementations must support.
